interview_outline:
The first round was a buddy call conducted by a recent MBA graduate working at the company. I was asked to give my introduction, explain my understanding of the role based on the PPT/JD, and share any questions I had.
The second buddy round was conducted by a Vice President and was slightly more technical. Both buddy rounds were held online.
Following these rounds, there was an offline networking and dinner round, which included two group discussions. Shortlisted candidates then appeared for a third interview. This was primarily an HR round, where I was asked questions such as: Why did you pursue an MBA? Why finance? What interests you about finance? Why do you want to pivot to finance after working in a completely different domain?
domain_questions: I was asked about my understanding of financial statements and whether I had reviewed the financial statements of any company. I was also asked to highlight anything noteworthy I had observed in those statements and answer a hypothetical question involving working capital and debt.
looking_for: They wanted someone who was sure about the role and was good in communication.
right_wrong: I was specifically asked, "Your UG and previous workex would be rendered useless, so is that something that you are comfortable with?" And I think I was a bit hesitant on the response.
tips: During the buddy round, demonstrating a willingness to learn can make a significant difference. The interviewers are aware of whether or not you have a finance background and tailor their questions accordingly. The GDs conducted during the dinner round were different from typical GDs; in my opinion, the quality of the points raised was given more importance than the quantity.

no_interviews_duration: 4, Junior Buddy Round - 40 minutes, Senior Buddy Round - 45 minutes, Director Round - 40 minutes, HR Round - 25 minutes
interview_outline:
Round 1: Buddy Round (about 40-45 minutes)
This round was with one of the buddies assigned to me during the process.
It was mostly technical and resume-based. They asked about whatever was on my resume, so know every line of it.
Since I'd done a chemicals internship and had worked on that area, I knew a lot of the content, and that made it easier.
Expect HR and situational questions too, such as how you'd prioritise work if different seniors gave you conflicting tasks, and what circumstances might change your approach.
"Why this bank?" and "Why IB?" come up in almost every round, so prepare them well.

Round 2: VP Round - Technical (about 50 minutes)
This was the longest round, and it was heavily technical.
It covered theory and practice, and they went deep into the resume. Prepare thoroughly for the technical fundamentals and the theory behind them.
It also included situational and HR questions.
"Why this bank?" and "Why IB?" came up again, along with broader versions like "Why not other banks?"
It helps to know the firm well beyond the basics, including the kinds of programmes and career paths it offers its people.

Round 3: Director Round (35 - 40 minutes)
It was light on technicals. I got a few finance questions, such as how return on capital relates to cost of capital and what it means when one is above or below the other. 
The focus was on HR and situational questions.
Go in with an open mind. They like testing how you handle workplace dilemmas, such as disagreements with colleagues. Think about how you'd handle them honestly and professionally. Make sure to get some learning out as well since this round can be very informative to know about the company.

Round 4: Final Round (HR) (about 25 minutes)
Mostly HR-style questions, such as what you learned in your internship and which two qualities describe you.
Situational questions can come up here too, and the conversation can go in different directions depending on the interviewer.
domain_questions:
A lot throughout the process- 
Read the through the red book and cover the topics that relate to the resume you make-
Topics like-
Statements of Accounting, Ratios and their implied meanings, DCF and its calculation, other methods of valuation such as relative valuation, etc can be extensively tested.
hr_gk_questions: The candidate should know about the happenings surrounding the company and the atmosphere of the the financial world. Movements in stock prices and industry dynamics are frequently asked as well.
prep_resources: Resources- Red Book, Stock Pitch (Economic Times industry report & stock analysis), Screener,  Prepcomm Primers, CFA materials.
looking_for:
They were looking at the following-
1. Communication Skills
2. Technical Depth and understanding
3. Culture Fit 
4. Love and preference for finance
right_wrong: Be careful in asking closing questions for clarification. They should be good and insightful. Also, don't keep too many questions just for the sake of asking them.
tips: A slight confident smile and relaxed posture, along with smart dressing always helps.
dos_and_donts:
Dos-
1. Be confident
2. Smile a little
3. Brush up financial concepts
4. Go with an open mind and eager to learn
5. Be to the point while answering the questions

Donts-
1. Dont sound overconfident
2. Dont ask unnecessary questions in the end

interview_outline:
**Round 1 (~30 minutes): A 20-minute quantitative case on a cosmetics company evaluating the effectiveness of different marketing campaigns, involving online/offline sales, discounts, revenue and margins. This was followed by ~10 minutes of HR questions about previous internships and experiences.

**Round 2 (~70 minutes): A ~60-minute business case on a blood-sample testing machine company facing slowing growth and profitability, exploring entry into the home glucose-monitoring market for diabetes patients. The case covered market sizing, future market growth, financial feasibility, profitability, break-even calculations and recommendations. The final ~10 minutes focused on technical skills and tools, including AI and Power BI.
domain_questions:
- What metrics would you use to evaluate the effectiveness of different marketing campaigns?
- How would you calculate revenue and margins across different campaign scenarios?
- How would you estimate the market size and future growth of home glucose-monitoring devices?
- How would you evaluate the financial feasibility and break-even point of entering a new market?
- What recommendations would you make based on the market and financial analysis?
- Questions about technical tools and skills, including AI and Power BI.
hr_gk_questions:
- Questions about my previous internships and experiences.
- Details about my responsibilities, work undertaken and key learnings from previous internships.
- Questions about my technical background and familiarity with AI and Power BI.

No specific current-affairs questions were recalled.
prep_resources: Practising consulting cases, market-sizing problems, profitability analysis, break-even calculations and mental maths. Revising previous internship experiences and preparing to explain technical skills and their practical business applications also helped.
looking_for: Strong quantitative aptitude, structured problem-solving, attention to detail, and the ability to interpret data in a business context. They appeared to value the ability to use all the information provided, perform calculations accurately, assess market attractiveness and financial feasibility, and arrive at practical recommendations. The technical discussion also indicated the importance of understanding tools such as AI and Power BI and their potential business applications.
right_wrong: The overall approach went well, as I covered the major aspects of both cases and utilised the information provided at the appropriate stages. I was able to structure the analysis, perform market-sizing calculations and evaluate financial feasibility. However, the second case was lengthy, and I made a few minor calculation errors towards the end. I could have been more patient, managed my time better and rechecked my calculations before arriving at the final recommendation.
tips: A structured approach, strong quantitative aptitude and attention to detail helped significantly. Using the data provided rather than making unnecessary assumptions was important. Practising market sizing, profitability and break-even analysis beforehand was useful. Explaining the reasoning behind calculations and connecting the results to business decisions also helped.
tech_skills: Quantitative Analysis, Market Sizing, Financial Modelling
dos_and_donts:
Do: Practise mental maths, market sizing, profitability and break-even calculations. Listen carefully to the assumptions, use the information provided at the right stages, structure your approach and explain your reasoning aloud. Prepare your internship experiences and be ready to discuss AI, Power BI and other technical tools you know.

Don't: Rush through calculations, overlook small details or apply frameworks mechanically. In lengthy cases, remain patient and reserve time to verify your calculations and ensure your final recommendation follows logically from the analysis.

interview_outline:
The process consisted of a single, comprehensive round combining both technical and HR components. The discussion was heavily driven by my resume and the specific requirements of the role. The interviewer focused on my undergraduate Mechanical Engineering specialization and how my prior industry experience tied into manufacturing operations.

It was a highly conversational yet probing interview—each question built directly on my previous answers. The role-based questions got quite technical, diving into the actual mechanics of how physical systems connect to digital frameworks. Anyone preparing for this role absolutely needs a deep, conceptual understanding of every term mentioned in the job description (like Digital Continuity, PLM, MES, and IoT integration) rather than just surface-level definitions.
domain_questions: This section was heavily role-based. The interviewer wanted to rigorously test my technical understanding of the job description and evaluate if I had the right conceptual depth to actually execute the project.
hr_gk_questions: There were no explicit HR or current affairs questions. Instead, the behavioral evaluation was completely woven into the technical discussion. They were primarily testing my communication style, my confidence when breaking down complex technical answers, and my genuine passion for the Industry 4.0 and Digital Twin space. Since this is a client-facing consulting role, how clearly you communicate a technical concept is just as important as the answer itself, and that is exactly what they were assessing.
prep_resources: The IIM Indore placement decks helped me structure my thoughts, while PrepChat testimonials gave me a realistic sense of the interview flow. Beyond that, simply mapping my prior manufacturing work experience to the Digital Twin concepts in the job description was my best preparation.
looking_for: Ultimately, they were looking for someone who could bridge the gap between shop-floor realities and digital strategy. They wanted a candidate who is technically grounded—someone with prior exposure to manufacturing or heavy industry. For a consulting role in Capgemini's Intelligent Industry practice, you need that hands-on background to truly understand a client's physical operations. Without that baseline, it is very difficult to accurately identify their actual business problems or propose viable Digital Twin adoption frameworks.
right_wrong: Overall, it was a very smooth, conversational interview. What went right was my ability to connect my past manufacturing/ Digital Engineering experience directly to their technical questions, which drove the discussion organically. At the end, I was also given the chance to ask a few questions, which was a great opportunity to show my genuine interest in the specific summer project.
tips: Thoroughly dissect the job description. You need to understand every technical concept they mention—like IoT, MES, or Digital Continuity—and how they tie into business strategy. It is also crucial to research the company's overall structure, specifically understanding the difference between Capgemini's general IT services and the Capgemini Invent consulting arm. They evaluate you holistically, so backing up your conceptual knowledge with a confident delivery is what will ultimately set you apart.
tech_skills: Digital Twin Architecture, Industry 4.0, and Discrete Manufacturing Operations.
dos_and_donts:
Do(s):

Do drive the interview using your past work experience. Whenever possible, tie their technical questions back to real examples from your shop-floor or engineering days.

Do ask a smart, role-specific question at the end to show you understand the consulting nature of Capgemini Invent.

Don’t(s):

Don't bluff technical jargon. Because the interview is highly conversational, they will immediately cross-question you if you drop a buzzword without knowing how it works.

Don't treat it purely as an IT interview. Remember this is a strategy consulting role—always tie the technology back to business value (ROI, cost reduction, efficiency).

Special Preparation:
Read a few actual Capgemini Invent case studies or whitepapers on Industry 4.0 and Digital Twins before the interview. Knowing their specific consulting frameworks or recent client successes gives you a massive edge.

Additionally, make sure you know (or have at least read up on) the major Digital Twin platforms in the market—like Siemens, Dassault Systèmes, and NVIDIA Omniverse. You should also have a basic grasp of the end-to-end architecture (how data flows from IoT sensors on the shop floor into enterprise systems like MES and PLM). Finally, brush up on the analysis side of things—specifically how to build maturity models and calculate the ROI to actually justify the tech investment to a client.

interview_outline:
The first round is actually a workshop-and-dinner round with the VP, Akshay; Abhishek Agarwal (Director); Priyanka (Director); and Nikita (VP, IIM Indore Alumnus). We discussed an entire deal and understood the basics of M&A. 
The second round was an intro round with my buddy, during which they discussed basic finance concepts and went over how to prepare for the subsequent rounds. 
The third round was with a VP, during which we discussed sector-related questions and recent M&A activity in the sectors. Basic questions from the red book are too related to valuation and DCF. 
I was not shortlisted for further rounds.
domain_questions: Red Book questions: definitions of the terms in WACC and cost of debt, cost of equity, which is riskier, and how to value a company. Industry-based questions related to various kinds of M&A in the respective sector.
hr_gk_questions: They asked why Finance, why Deutsche Bank, and how many hours you are willing to give to the company.
looking_for: They were definitely looking for someone who had a background in finance and were well-versed with the theory.
right_wrong: Needed more depth of preparation in valuation concepts. But even when I used terms like "money transfer" instead of "cash flow," that was also okay because my concept was clear.
tips: Clarity of concept: how one part of the equation affects another, the relation between the various metrics.
tech_skills: Basic Accounting, Ratios and Values, and Valuations
dos_and_donts: Prepare your resume and be clear on your "whys." Try to relate everything to a finance concept and look for relevant examples in all scenarios.
